name: Dimethylcurcumin (ASC-J9)
lead: Dimethylcurcumin, known by the development code ASC-J9 (and also GO-Y025), is a synthetic curcumin derivative described as a nonsteroidal antiandrogen. Unlike conventional androgen receptor (AR) blockers, it is reported to work by promoting degradation of the androgen receptor protein rather than only occupying the receptor.[1][2] It is listed as an experimental drug and is not approved for any use.[1]

In appearance-related contexts it has been of interest as a topical anti-androgen for acne. Two Phase 2 trials of an ASC-J9 cream in acne were registered on ClinicalTrials.gov, one starting in 2007 with 186 participants and one in 2011 with 181 participants.[3][4] Both are listed as completed, but no peer-reviewed results for them are among the sources reviewed for this article, so its effect on acne in humans is not established in the published literature found here.

Most published work on ASC-J9 is laboratory and animal research, led by the group of Chawnshang Chang, in areas such as prostate cancer, spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy, bladder and liver cancer models, and wound healing.[5][6][7][8]

paras: Wikipedia describes ASC-J9 as inhibiting the androgen receptor in vitro without being a conventional antagonist; instead it appears to enhance AR degradation, apparently acting on particular AR populations.[1] A 2007 Nature Medicine paper reported that it reduced AR protein levels and improved the phenotype in a mouse model of spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy.[6] Later preclinical papers reported it degrading both full-length and splice-variant androgen receptors in castration-resistant prostate cancer cell models.[9][10]

Because it targets AR protein levels in tissues where AR is expressed, researchers have proposed that it could act locally in skin when applied topically, which is the rationale for the acne studies; this is a hypothesis about the design of the trials rather than a demonstrated result.

Two Phase 2 trials of topical ASC-J9 cream in acne are registered: NCT00525499 (acne vulgaris, started August 2007, 186 participants) and NCT01289574 (acne, started February 2011, 181 participants). Both are listed as completed.[3][4] No published results from either trial were found among the sources reviewed, so no efficacy or safety figures can be reported here.

Preclinical studies attribute a range of effects to AR signaling that ASC-J9 is used to probe. In mice, AR deletion or suppression has been linked to altered bladder cancer development, liver cancer development, hepatitis B-related liver tumour formation, and cutaneous wound healing speed.[5][7][8][11] Studies in prostate cancer models reported that ASC-J9 and the clinically used AR antagonists enzalutamide and bicalutamide had opposite effects on metastasis-related macrophage signaling.[12] These are animal and cell findings and have not been established in people.
ASC-J9 has also been tested in preclinical models of benign prostatic hyperplasia-related AR biology and in enzalutamide-resistant prostate cancer models.[9][13]

card.summary: An experimental curcumin-derived anti-androgen that breaks down the androgen receptor; tried as an acne cream in two Phase 2 trials with no published results found.
card.note: Not approved anywhere; human acne trial results are not published in the sources reviewed.

quick.overview:
ASC-J9 (dimethylcurcumin) is an experimental, curcumin-derived compound that lowers androgen receptor levels rather than just blocking the receptor. It has been studied in labs for prostate cancer and other conditions, and as a topical cream for acne.

Two Phase 2 acne trials (2007 and 2011, around 180 participants each) are registered as completed, but no published results were found, so its effect on acne in people is unestablished.
quick.mechanism: It is described as an androgen receptor degradation enhancer: it appears to reduce the amount of AR protein in cells, which is the idea behind using it on skin where androgens contribute to acne.
quick.risks: It is experimental and not approved by regulators. Human safety data from the acne trials are not published in the sources reviewed; most other data come from cell and animal studies.
